title: Isaias Leaves Four Dead and Thousands Without Power in the US
seoTitle: Isaias Leaves Four Dead, Thousands Without Power in US
subtitle: Post-Tropical Storm Causes Strong Winds, Flooding, and Destruction in Florida, Alabama, and Other Southern States
excerpt: Isaias' passage leaves four dead, tens of thousands of homes without power, and a risk of new floods as the cyclone moves inland across the United States.
author: Daniele Morais
sourceName: FOX Weather, BBC, The Weather Channel
contentHtml:
In the early hours of Friday, Cyclone Isaias made landfall on the Florida coast as a Category 2 hurricane, with winds up to 105 mph (168 km/h). The immediate impact caused fallen trees, ripped-off roofs, and power outages already affecting approximately 500,000 people across several states.

Victims and Destruction in Affected Areas

Two deaths were recorded in Florida and two in Alabama, all resulting from trees falling on homes. In Escambia, Florida, a woman died when a tree trunk collapsed her home's roof. In another incident, a man passed away from carbon monoxide poisoning while using a generator indoors.

Extent of Outages and Restoration Efforts

More than 400,000 customers remained without power on Saturday night, according to electric utility data. Florida Power & Light has already reconnected approximately 98,000 customers and aims to restore power to 95% of those affected by the end of Monday. In Alabama, over 125,000 homes also lost electricity.

Intense Rainfall and Risk of Further Flooding

The Weather Prediction Center indicated that the system will continue to generate heavy rainfall across the Southeast and Southern Appalachians, with accumulations of 2 to 5 inches and isolated peaks of up to 10 inches. Flood and high wind warnings remain in effect, particularly in the coastal regions of North and South Carolina.

Possible Formation of a "Sting Jet" and Concentrated Damage

Analysts at the FOX Forecast Center indicate that Isaias was already transitioning into a non-tropical cyclone upon making landfall, favoring the formation of a "sting jet" – a narrow corridor of extremely intense winds that may have caused the most severe damage west of the storm's center, contrary to the typical hurricane pattern.

Outlook for the Cyclone's Trajectory

After losing its tropical structure, Isaias is moving towards Tennessee, maintaining winds of up to 25 mph and still carrying a large volume of moisture. The system is expected to advance into the Northeastern United States in the coming days, where it will continue to generate rain and a risk of severe storms, before being absorbed by another low-pressure system.

With information from FOX Weather, BBC, The Weather Channel.
